prompt: Systems Development Methodology is MOST accurately defined as:

options.text: A regulatory compliance framework mandating the documentation standards for government information systems
The set of hardware and software tools used by developers to construct and test information systems
The standard process followed by an organisation to conduct all the steps necessary to analyse, design, implement, and maintain information systems
A specific programming language or development framework chosen by an organisation for building software

explanation: A methodology is a PROCESS, not a product and not a toolset. It is the organisation's standard way of getting from a business need to a working, maintained system, and it names the steps, their order, and what each must produce. Waterfall, RAD, Agile and the spiral are all methodologies because each answers the same question differently: in what order do we analyse, design, implement and maintain.

why.a: Wrong. Compliance frameworks constrain how you document; they do not tell you how to develop.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the commonest confusion: those are CASE tools. Tools support a methodology, they are not one.
why.c: Correct. Standard process, covering analyse, design, implement and maintain.
why.d: Wrong. The language is an implementation choice made INSIDE a methodology.

prompt: The 'get the user involved' principle in successful systems development emphasises that user involvement throughout the process:

options.text: Is only necessary for consumer-facing systems and not required for internal back-office applications
Should be limited to the initial requirements phase to prevent users from disrupting the technical development work
Helps ensure that requirements are accurate, reduces resistance to change, and increases user acceptance of the final system
Increases development costs significantly but is mandatory for regulatory compliance in most industries

explanation: Three benefits, and the question wants all three: accuracy, less resistance, more acceptance. Users are the only people who know what the work actually involves, so keeping them in the room is how requirements stay true. The second and third benefits are political rather than technical: a system people helped shape is a system people will use.

why.a: Wrong. Internal systems fail for exactly the same reason, and their users are easier to reach.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the mistake the principle exists to prevent. Requirements change, and users are the ones who notice.
why.c: Correct. Accuracy, reduced resistance, and acceptance.
why.d: Wrong on both halves: involvement REDUCES the cost of rework, and it is good practice rather than a regulation.

prompt: The Waterfall Model is characterised by which of the following fundamental features?

options.text: A traditional, linear approach in which each phase must be completed before the next phase begins, with key deliverables presented for approval at each phase end
A flexible framework that allows requirements to evolve and development activities to be revisited throughout the project
An iterative development cycle where system components are built, tested, and refined through multiple rapid iterations
A collaborative approach that integrates users into every phase of development through continuous prototyping and feedback

explanation: Linear, sequential, and gated. Water falls downhill and does not flow back up, which is the whole image: finish a phase, get it approved, and only then start the next. Its strength is control and documentation; its weakness is that a requirement discovered late is expensive, because going back means going back a long way.

why.a: Correct. Linear, each phase complete before the next, deliverables approved at each gate.
why.b: Wrong. That flexibility describes the ADAPTIVE approaches, which exist because Waterfall lacks it.
why.c: Wrong. That is iterative or incremental development.
why.d: Wrong. Continuous prototyping and user integration describe RAD and JAD.

prompt: Building a system based on incomplete or misunderstood requirements is MOST likely to result in which of the following outcomes?

options.text: Over budgeting, late delivery, or delivery of a system that does not fully solve the problems it was intended to address
Improved system performance but with reduced functionality compared to what users originally requested
Increased user satisfaction because a simpler system is easier to learn and operate
Faster delivery due to reduced scope, though with some features deferred to a future release

explanation: Bad requirements are the most expensive defect in the whole life cycle, because everything downstream is built on them. The error is not discovered until testing or delivery, by which time the design, the code and the data structures have all committed to it. That is why fact-finding gets its own phase rather than being folded into design.

why.a: Correct. Over budget, late, and still not solving the problem.
why.b: Wrong. Misunderstanding requirements does not improve performance; it wastes effort on the wrong thing.
why.c: Wrong, and it confuses a system that is SMALLER by accident with one that is SIMPLER by design.
why.d: Wrong. Deferring scope on purpose is a plan. Misunderstanding it is not, and it costs time rather than saving it.

prompt: What is the key purpose of the 'Joint Application Development (JAD)' technique as it relates to prototyping?

options.text: JAD replaces prototyping entirely by using structured group meetings to eliminate the need for visual demonstrations
JAD produces the final system without any prototyping by having all stakeholders simultaneously define and approve requirements
JAD is used exclusively during the implementation phase to coordinate the joint efforts of developers and testers
When JRP/JAD incorporates prototyping as a means for confirming requirements and obtaining design approvals, the benefits of prototyping are realised within a structured group collaboration framework

explanation: JAD and prototyping are partners, not rivals. JAD puts users, analysts and managers in one room to agree requirements quickly; a prototype gives that room something concrete to react to, because people criticise a screen far better than they criticise a paragraph. Put them together and you confirm requirements AND obtain design approval in the same session.

why.a: Wrong. It uses prototyping rather than eliminating it.
why.b: Wrong. JAD gathers and agrees requirements; it does not produce the finished system.
why.c: Wrong phase. JAD belongs to requirements and design, not implementation.
why.d: Correct. Prototyping inside a structured group framework, confirming requirements and gaining approvals.

prompt: How does the adaptive approach to SDLC fundamentally differ from the predictive approach in handling requirements?

options.text: The adaptive approach requires more extensive documentation than the predictive approach to manage changing requirements
The adaptive approach relies entirely on automated tools to manage requirements, while the predictive approach depends on manual documentation

In the adaptive approach, requirements evolve over time through continuous user feedback and incremental delivery, whereas the predictive approach defines requirements upfront before development begins
The adaptive approach follows a fixed sequential process while the predictive approach allows for iterative development cycles

explanation: The names say it. PREDICTIVE predicts: it decides everything at the start and then follows the plan, which suits projects where the requirements are genuinely known and stable. ADAPTIVE adapts: it expects requirements to change, so it delivers in increments and lets feedback reshape what comes next.

why.a: Wrong. Adaptive approaches deliberately favour working software over heavy documentation.
why.b: Wrong. Neither is defined by its tooling.
why.c: Correct. Evolving through feedback and increments, against fixed upfront definition.
why.d: Wrong, and it is exactly backwards. The fixed sequential process is the PREDICTIVE one.

prompt: Which of the following BEST explains the 'justify systems as capital investments' principle in systems development?

options.text: All information systems should be classified as capital assets on the organisation's balance sheet for tax purposes
Information systems should be replaced on a fixed capital depreciation schedule regardless of their operational effectiveness

Information systems require significant financial resources and should be evaluated like other capital investments using cost-benefit analysis to determine whether expected benefits justify the costs and risks involved
Systems analysts must obtain capital funding approval from shareholders before any development activities can commence

explanation: A system competes for money with every other thing the organisation could buy, so it has to earn its place the same way: cost-benefit analysis, weighed against risk. This is why economic feasibility exists as a study in its own right, and why an analyst who cannot express benefits in money has not finished the argument.

why.a: Wrong. Accounting classification is not the principle; the principle is about JUSTIFYING the spend.
why.b: Wrong. Replacement on a schedule ignores whether the system still works, which is the opposite of evaluating it.
why.c: Correct. Evaluate like any capital investment, using cost-benefit analysis against costs and risks.
why.d: Wrong. Shareholder approval is not what this means, and few projects would ever start.

prompt: Which of the following is a recognised ADVANTAGE of the RAD methodology?

options.text: RAD is best suited for safety-critical systems because it emphasises rigorous testing at every development phase
RAD produces the most comprehensive technical documentation of any methodology, supporting long-term maintenance
User feedback makes the model very effective, a time-box approach mitigates cost and schedule risk, and development costs are lower because the system matches user expectations
RAD eliminates all project risks by freezing requirements at the beginning and adhering strictly to the original scope

explanation: Rapid Application Development buys speed with user contact and a fixed clock. The TIME BOX is the key idea: the deadline is fixed and the scope flexes to fit, which is the reverse of Waterfall and is what keeps cost and schedule risk contained. Costs fall because rework falls, since users have been correcting the thing all along.

why.a: Wrong. Safety-critical work goes to the V-model, which pairs a test with every phase.
why.b: Wrong, and it is RAD's best-known DISADVANTAGE: speed comes at the cost of documentation.
why.c: Correct. User feedback, the time box, and lower cost through fewer surprises.
why.d: Wrong. Freezing requirements is Waterfall's approach, and no method eliminates all risk.

prompt: When a systems analyst is said to be performing 'system design', what is the analyst primarily doing?

options.text: Translating requirements identified during system analysis into a detailed blueprint that specifies how the system will be structured and how its components will interact
Gathering requirements from users through interviews, questionnaires, and observation
Studying the existing business processes to identify inefficiencies and problem areas
Testing the completed system to verify it meets functional and non-functional specifications

explanation: Analysis asks WHAT the system must do; design answers HOW it will do it. The handover between them is the moment requirements become a blueprint: structure, components, and the way those components talk to each other. If you can keep what against how straight, four exam questions answer themselves.

why.a: Correct. Requirements turned into a blueprint of structure and interaction.
why.b: Wrong. That is fact-finding, which belongs to ANALYSIS.
why.c: Wrong. Studying the current system is analysis too, earlier still.
why.d: Wrong. That is testing, which comes after implementation.

prompt: Systems design specifications are best described as documents that:

options.text: Outline the business problems and high-level requirements gathered during the analysis phase
Describe the construction details of all system components including databases, networks, program modules, operating procedures, user interfaces, and conversion plans
Record the testing outcomes and user acceptance results following system implementation
Document the feasibility study results including economic, technical, and operational assessments

explanation: A design specification is a builder's document: detailed enough that somebody else could construct the system from it. Learn the list, because the examiner uses it: databases, networks, program modules, operating procedures, user interfaces, and conversion plans. Notice that it covers the changeover too, not only the software.

why.a: Wrong. High-level problems and requirements belong to the analysis phase that came before.
why.b: Correct. Construction detail across all six areas.
why.c: Wrong. Test results come after the build.
why.d: Wrong. Feasibility is a study done early to decide whether to proceed at all.

prompt: Which of the following BEST describes why developing information systems without a clear methodology is problematic?

options.text: It is only problematic for large organisations; small organisations can successfully develop systems without a formal methodology
It always results in technically superior systems because developers have greater creative freedom without constraints
It reduces the time to market but typically produces systems with excessive documentation and redundant features
It often leads to cost overruns, missed deadlines, and systems that fail to meet user requirements

explanation: Three symptoms, and they are the same three the whole course keeps returning to: over cost, over time, and under-delivering. A methodology is not bureaucracy for its own sake; it is the thing that makes each of those failures visible early enough to fix, by naming what must be produced and approved before the next step begins.

why.a: Wrong. Size changes the weight of the process, not the need for one.
why.b: Wrong. Freedom without structure is what produces the failures listed in the correct option.
why.c: Wrong on both counts, and it is self-contradictory: skipping a methodology does not generate excessive documentation.
why.d: Correct. Cost overruns, missed deadlines, and systems that miss the requirement.

prompt: According to the methodology selection criteria, which approach is BEST suited for projects with very short time schedules?

options.text: The V-Shape Model, because its emphasis on testing from the start prevents costly defect correction near the deadline
The Parallel Model, because dividing the system into independent subprojects allows concurrent development tracks
The Waterfall model, because its structured sequential approach prevents time-wasting rework between phases

RAD methodologies, because they are designed to accelerate development, with iterative development and system prototyping allowing the team to adjust system functionality to meet a specific delivery date

explanation: The clue is in the name: RAD is RAPID Application Development, and short schedules are the problem it was built for. The mechanism is the time box, which fixes the date and flexes the functionality, so the team adjusts what ships rather than when it ships. Learn the selection criteria as a table of problem against answer, because this examiner asks it repeatedly.

why.a: Wrong. The V-model suits RELIABILITY, not speed; all that testing takes time.
why.b: Wrong. The Parallel model shortens the schedule somewhat, but RAD is the one the criteria name for very short schedules.
why.c: Wrong, and backwards: Waterfall is the slowest to first delivery because nothing ships until the end.
why.d: Correct. Built for speed, using iteration, prototyping, and a fixed delivery date.

prompt: The principle 'establish standards for development and documentation' in successful systems development serves which primary purpose?

options.text: To ensure consistency, quality, and clarity across system development activities, making systems easier to understand, maintain, and enhance over time
To satisfy external regulatory bodies that mandate specific documentation formats for audit and compliance purposes
To ensure all development teams use identical programming languages and database management systems
To create bureaucratic checkpoints that prevent developers from making unauthorised changes to system requirements

explanation: Standards exist for the person who comes after you. Most of a system's life is MAINTENANCE, carried out by people who were not in the room when it was built, and consistent practice plus clear documentation is what makes that possible. Consistency, quality, clarity, then maintainability: that chain is the answer.

why.a: Correct. Consistency and clarity now, maintainability and enhancement later.
why.b: Wrong. Compliance may be a side benefit, but it is not the purpose.
why.c: Wrong. Standards govern HOW work is done and documented, not which tools are used.
why.d: Wrong, and it describes change control as an obstacle rather than the principle's aim.

prompt: The Incremental Model is BEST described as a methodology that:

options.text: Builds the entire system in one continuous development cycle before delivering it to users for acceptance testing
Develops the system in small, manageable portions called increments, where each increment adds new functionality and builds on previous releases, combining linear and iterative approaches
Develops the system by having multiple teams work on competing implementations, with the best solution selected at project completion
Requires all requirements to be undefined at project start, with features discovered entirely through user interaction with prototypes

explanation: Increments are slices of working system, each one adding function to what is already delivered. The phrase worth memorising is that it COMBINES linear and iterative: each increment runs a small waterfall inside it, while the sequence of increments is iterative. That is why it delivers value early without abandoning structure.

why.a: Wrong. One big delivery at the end is Waterfall.
why.b: Correct. Small increments, each building on the last, linear and iterative together.
why.c: Wrong. Competing teams describes nothing in this course.
why.d: Wrong, and too extreme: increments still need requirements, just not all of them at once.

prompt: Which of the following statements about the Waterfall model's documentation is accurate?

options.text: The Waterfall model's documentation is informal and maintained only by developers without requiring management approval
The Waterfall model produces extensive written documentation and requires formal reviews and user and IT management sign-off at the end of each phase to ensure strict monitoring
The Waterfall model intentionally minimises documentation to keep teams focused on delivering working software quickly
The Waterfall model produces documentation only at the implementation phase when the system is ready for user acceptance

explanation: Documentation is Waterfall's defining strength and its defining cost. Each phase ends with a deliverable, that deliverable is formally reviewed, and BOTH user and IT management sign it off before the next phase starts. Those sign-off gates are what make the model auditable, and also what make change expensive once a gate has closed.

why.a: Wrong. Formal approval at each gate is the model's central control.
why.b: Correct. Extensive documentation, formal review, and sign-off by user and IT management at each phase end.
why.c: Wrong. Minimising documentation is the AGILE preference, and it is Waterfall's opposite.
why.d: Wrong. Documentation is produced throughout, phase by phase.

prompt: According to the analyst's problem-solving approach, what must the analyst do FIRST before recommending any solution?

options.text: Develop a set of possible alternative solutions and present them to management for selection
Confirm with management that the benefits of solving the problem outweigh the associated costs
Research and thoroughly understand the problem, including who is involved, what business processes are affected, and what other systems would be impacted
Define the detailed design specifications and create a blueprint for the new system

explanation: Understand before you solve. The steps run in order: research and understand the problem, then verify that the benefits of solving it outweigh the costs, then develop alternatives, then recommend. Every wrong option here is a LATER step in that same sequence, which is the trap: they are all things the analyst does, just not first.

why.a: Wrong step, and it comes third. You cannot generate alternatives to a problem you have not understood.
why.b: Wrong step, and it comes second. Cost-benefit follows understanding.
why.c: Correct. Understand the problem, who is involved, which processes and which other systems are affected.
why.d: Wrong phase entirely. Design comes long after the problem is understood and a solution chosen.

prompt: In the adaptive SDLC approach, what is a 'sprint' and what does it produce?

options.text: A specialised testing cycle conducted after each major release to identify and resolve performance deficiencies
A planning meeting held at the start of the project to define the complete set of system requirements
An accelerated version of the waterfall model where all phases are compressed into a single two-week period
A short, time-boxed development cycle that includes analysis, design, coding, testing, and review, producing a working increment of the system at its conclusion

explanation: A sprint is a whole miniature project: it contains every activity, from analysis through review, and it ends with something that WORKS. Two features carry the marks. It is TIME-BOXED, so the clock is fixed and the scope moves, and it produces a working increment rather than a document or a phase.

why.a: Wrong. Testing happens inside a sprint, not after releases as a separate cycle.
why.b: Wrong. Defining all requirements upfront is the predictive approach a sprint exists to avoid.
why.c: Wrong, and it is the tempting one: a sprint is not a compressed waterfall, because it repeats and adapts rather than running once.
why.d: Correct. Short, time-boxed, all activities included, ending in a working increment.

prompt: Which of the following is a DISADVANTAGE of evolutionary prototyping?

options.text: It completely prevents users from seeing system requirements as they are being gathered, reducing accuracy
It has a tendency to abandon structured program development for 'code-and-fix' development, overall maintainability may be overlooked, and the process may continue forever due to scope creep
It produces excessive formal documentation that slows down the development process and increases overhead costs
It requires all requirements to be fully specified before any prototype can be developed and evaluated

explanation: Three named dangers, and the question wants all three: the slide into code-and-fix, maintainability being forgotten, and a process that never ends because every demonstration produces new requests. That last one has a name worth knowing: SCOPE CREEP. The prototype becomes the product without ever having been designed to be one.

why.a: Wrong, and inverted: letting users SEE the system early is prototyping's main advantage.
why.b: Correct. Code-and-fix, neglected maintainability, and endless scope creep.
why.c: Wrong. Prototyping produces too LITTLE documentation, not too much.
why.d: Wrong. Prototyping exists precisely because requirements cannot all be specified upfront.

prompt: The Parallel Model differs from the traditional Waterfall model primarily in which way?

options.text: The Parallel Model requires two separate development teams to work on different versions of the system for competitive evaluation
The Parallel Model introduces a dedicated testing phase that runs concurrently with every development phase from the beginning
The Parallel Model allows requirements to evolve during development through continuous user feedback and iterative enhancements
The overall system is divided into subprojects after the general analysis and high-level design phases, with each subproject moving through remaining phases simultaneously before integration

explanation: The split happens AFTER general analysis and high-level design, which is the detail the examiner is testing. You analyse and design the whole once, then break it into subprojects that run their remaining phases side by side, then integrate. That shortens the schedule without the subprojects contradicting one another, because they share one design.

why.a: Wrong. Competing versions is not what parallel means here.
why.b: Wrong. Testing alongside every phase is the V-MODEL.
why.c: Wrong. Evolving requirements describes the adaptive approaches.
why.d: Correct. Divided into subprojects after general analysis and high-level design, then integrated.

prompt: Which of the following BEST describes the primary objective of the design phase in the SDLC?

options.text: To monitor the installed system and make enhancements in response to changing business requirements
To construct software components, verify and test the system, and prepare it for deployment to users
To gather information from stakeholders and define the functional requirements of the new system
To design the solution system based on requirements defined during analysis, developing an architectural structure for software components, databases, user interfaces, and the operating environment

explanation: Design turns WHAT into HOW, and the four things it structures are worth memorising as a list: software components, databases, user interfaces, and the operating environment. Every wrong option here is a different SDLC phase, so this question is really asking whether you can name the phases apart.

why.a: Wrong. Monitoring and enhancing is SUPPORT, the phase after implementation.
why.b: Wrong. Building and testing is IMPLEMENTATION.
why.c: Wrong. Gathering and defining requirements is ANALYSIS.
why.d: Correct. Architectural structure for components, databases, interfaces and the operating environment.

prompt: In the table comparing methodology usefulness, which methodology is rated 'Excellent' for projects with UNCLEAR user requirements?

options.text: The V-Model is rated Excellent because its rigorous testing phases help uncover hidden or unclear requirements
Waterfall and Parallel models are rated Excellent because their structured approach forces requirements clarification
The Iterative model alone is rated Excellent while all other methodologies are rated Poor for unclear requirements
System Prototyping, Throwaway Prototyping, and Agile Development are all rated Excellent for unclear user requirements

explanation: All three work the same way: they put something in front of the user EARLY, so the requirement gets discovered by reaction rather than by description. The manual says it plainly on page 41: when requirements are unclear, system prototyping and throwaway prototyping are more appropriate, because they provide prototypes for users to interact with early in the SDLC. Agile joins them because each sprint delivers something a user can react to.

why.a: Wrong. The V-model tests against requirements you already have; it cannot discover ones nobody has stated.
why.b: Wrong, and backwards. Structure DEMANDS clear requirements rather than producing them.
why.c: Wrong. It is not one methodology alone, and the others are not all rated Poor.
why.d: Correct. All three let users interact with something early, which is how unclear requirements become clear.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT listed as a popular Agile methodology in the course material?

options.text: Critical Path Method (CPM)
Scrum
Extreme Programming (XP)
Kanban

explanation: The manual lists five popular agile methods on page 40: Crystal Clear, Scrum, Extreme Programming, Lean Software Development, and Kanban. The Critical Path Method is a PROJECT SCHEDULING technique for working out which chain of tasks determines the finish date. It is a planning tool, not a development methodology, and it belongs to the predictive world rather than the agile one.

why.a: Correct, this is the odd one out. CPM is a scheduling technique, not an agile method.
why.b: Wrong, it is on the list, and it is the best known of the five.
why.c: Wrong, it is on the list.
why.d: Wrong, it is on the list.

prompt: The principle of 'divide and conquer' in systems development MOST closely corresponds to which analytical concept?

options.text: Separating business requirements from technical specifications to prevent scope creep during development
Breaking a large system into smaller, manageable components or subsystems to simplify development and reduce complexity
Dividing the project budget equally among planning, analysis, design, and implementation phases
Distributing system development work among multiple competing vendor teams to accelerate delivery

explanation: Divide and conquer is functional decomposition wearing its everyday name. Break the system into subsystems, let each team hold one part in their head, and make sure the parts still work as a whole. The same idea drives levelled data flow diagrams, where one process on a Level 0 diagram becomes a whole Level 1 diagram of its own.

why.a: Wrong. That separation is useful but it is not what dividing and conquering means.
why.b: Correct. Smaller manageable components, simpler development, less complexity.
why.c: Wrong. Nothing in the principle concerns budget allocation.
why.d: Wrong. Competing vendors is not decomposition; it is duplication.

prompt: The 'support phase' of the SDLC is MOST accurately described as:

options.text: Activities to upgrade and maintain the system after deployment, including fixing bugs, making enhancements, and supporting users through a help desk
The process of conducting feasibility studies and producing the initial project proposal for management approval
The phase where analysts gather and document user requirements before system design begins
The activities carried out during system construction to ensure technical components meet design specifications

explanation: Three activities, and the question names all three: maintain, enhance, support. MAINTAIN means fixing bugs and making minor adjustments. ENHANCE means the bigger changes forced by new regulations, new competition or new infrastructure. SUPPORT means the help desk. Remember too that support is part of the overall SDLC but is not normally counted as part of the initial development project.

why.a: Correct. Upgrade and maintain after deployment, with bug fixing, enhancement and the help desk.
why.b: Wrong. Feasibility and the project proposal belong to PLANNING.
why.c: Wrong. Gathering and documenting requirements is ANALYSIS.
why.d: Wrong. Construction against design specifications is IMPLEMENTATION.

prompt: Why is testing considered one of the most critical steps in the implementation phase of the SDLC?

options.text: Because testing generates the official documentation required for regulatory compliance and audit purposes
Because the cost of bugs can be immense, and most organisations spend more time and attention on testing than on writing the programs in the first place
Because testing determines the final project budget and influences decisions about future system enhancements
Because testing is the only phase where users are directly involved in the system development process

explanation: This is page 22 word for word, and the striking half is the second one: more time goes on testing than on writing the programs. The reason is economic rather than technical. A defect caught in testing costs a fix; the same defect caught by a customer costs the fix plus the damage plus the trust, which is why organisations spend where they do.

why.a: Wrong. Documentation is a by-product, not the reason.
why.b: Correct. The cost of bugs, and more effort spent testing than programming.
why.c: Wrong. Budget decisions belong to planning, and are revised throughout.
why.d: Wrong. Users are involved throughout, most heavily in analysis.

prompt: The concept of 'functional decomposition' in systems analysis refers to:

options.text: The approach of dividing a system into smaller, manageable components or subsystems to focus analysis on individual areas of a business
The method of assigning different system functions to separate teams of developers during implementation
The process of documenting the functional requirements of a system in a structured specification document
The technique of breaking down a user's functional requirements into technical design specifications

explanation: Functional decomposition is the analyst's basic move: a system contains subsystems, and those contain subsystems of their own. It lets you focus on one area of the business, on a group of related areas, or on the interfaces between them. Note the trap in the wrong options: decomposition divides the SYSTEM, not the work, the document, or the requirements.

why.a: Correct. Dividing the system into subsystems so analysis can focus on one area at a time.
why.b: Wrong. That divides the TEAM, which is a management decision.
why.c: Wrong. That is writing a requirements specification.
why.d: Wrong. That is the analysis-to-design translation, a different step.

prompt: The Waterfall model is MOST suitable for which type of project scenario?

options.text: A large, expensive, and complicated project with clear objectives, stable and comprehensive requirements, and no pressure for immediate implementation
A startup environment where rapid prototyping and quick delivery of a minimum viable product are the primary goals
A project with frequently changing customer requirements that demand continuous user feedback and iterative delivery
A project where the development team is highly experienced with agile techniques and self-organising workflows

explanation: Straight from page 30's list of when to use Waterfall. Every clause matters: LARGE and complicated, because the structure pays for itself at scale; CLEAR objectives and STABLE requirements, because going back is expensive; and NO pressure for immediate implementation, because nothing ships until the end. The list adds one more worth knowing: Waterfall also suits teams that are inexperienced or may change during implementation, because the documentation carries the knowledge.

why.a: Correct, and it matches the manual's list clause for clause.
why.b: Wrong. Rapid delivery of a minimum viable product is RAD or Agile.
why.c: Wrong, and it is Waterfall's worst case: changing requirements are what it handles badly.
why.d: Wrong. An experienced agile team is a reason to use Agile.

prompt: The principle 'design systems for growth and change' in successful systems development is MOST concerned with:

options.text: Ensuring systems are flexible and scalable to accommodate future business expansion, technological advancements, and changing user requirements, thereby extending the system's useful life
Building systems exclusively on the latest technology platforms regardless of organisational budget constraints
Designing systems with the maximum number of features possible so future enhancements are not needed
Establishing rigid technical standards that prevent unauthorised modifications to the system after deployment

explanation: Two words carry it: FLEXIBLE and SCALABLE. Three things change over a system's life, and the manual names them all: the business expands, the technology moves, and users want different things. Designing for that extends the system's useful life, which protects the money already spent. That last clause is why this principle sits beside justifying systems as capital investments.

why.a: Correct. Flexible and scalable, for expansion, new technology and changing requirements.
why.b: Wrong. Newest is not the same as adaptable, and budget always constrains.
why.c: Wrong, and it is the opposite: cramming in features now does not remove the need to change later.
why.d: Wrong. Rigidity prevents change rather than accommodating it.

prompt: Throwaway (rapid or exploratory) prototyping is MOST appropriate when:

options.text: The project has well-understood and stable requirements that are unlikely to change during the development lifecycle
The organisation requires the highest possible system reliability and has zero tolerance for defects in production
The development team is highly experienced and needs no exploratory phase before committing to the final design
There is a lack of familiarity with the technology, requirements are unclear, or there are complex technical risks that must be explored through design prototypes before the actual system is built

explanation: Throwaway prototyping is a RISK tool. You build something disposable precisely where you do not yet know enough: an unfamiliar technology, a requirement nobody can state, a technical problem that might not have a solution. You learn the answer, you throw the prototype away, and you then build the real system properly with a structured methodology.

why.a: Wrong. Stable, well-understood requirements are the case for Waterfall.
why.b: Wrong here, though it is genuinely tempting: the manual DOES say throwaway prototyping suits high reliability. But the question asks when it is most appropriate overall, and unfamiliarity, unclear requirements and technical risk are the criteria the manual names first.
why.c: Wrong. If no exploration is needed, there is nothing for a throwaway prototype to do.
why.d: Correct. Unfamiliar technology, unclear requirements, or complex technical risks explored before the real build.

prompt: When system reliability is a HIGH priority, for example in medical equipment or missile control systems, which methodology is MOST appropriate according to the selection criteria?

options.text: RAD, because its time-box approach ensures rapid delivery of reliable system increments to users
Agile development, because its iterative nature allows defects to be detected and corrected after each sprint
The Incremental Model, because delivering high-risk functions first ensures the most critical components are reliable
The V-model, which is useful when reliability is important because it emphasises testing at each development phase through verification and validation

explanation:
The V-model pairs EVERY development phase with its own testing phase: down the left side you build, up the right side you verify and validate. Nothing is deferred to a test at the end. Medical equipment and missile control are the manual's own examples of critical reliability, against games and internet video where it is merely important.

One honest note. Page 41 says throwaway prototyping is most appropriate when reliability is a high priority, and that the V-model is useful when reliability is important. Throwaway prototyping is not offered here, so the V-model is the intended answer, and it is the right one among the four given.

why.a: Wrong. RAD trades quality for speed, which is the wrong trade for safety-critical work.
why.b: Wrong. Detecting defects AFTER each sprint is later than a safety-critical system can afford.
why.c: Wrong. Ordering the work by risk is not the same as verifying every phase.
why.d: Correct. Verification and validation built into every phase, which is what V stands for.
